Report a Sequential Procedure in Words

Source: R/seq_report.R
seq_report.Rd

Turns the result of a sequential procedure into a short paragraph that can be pasted into a methods or results section: the procedure and its source, its target (the confidence interval width and confidence level, or the loss constants), the sample size at which the stopping rule was met (or that it has not yet been met), and the estimate with its confidence interval. The full reference for the procedure is returned with the paragraph.

Usage

seq_report(x, digits = 3L)

# S3 method for class 'smsd_report'
format(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'smsd_report'
print(x, width = 0.9 * getOption("width"), ...)

Arguments

x

For seq_report(): an object of class "smsd_check", as returned by a sequential check function (for example seq_aipe_smd or seq_mr_cv), or of class "smsd_path", as returned by seq_path. For format() and print(): the report that seq_report() returned.

digits

The number of decimal places shown for the estimate and its confidence limits. A whole number from 0 to 15; default 3. This affects the text only: nothing stored in x is rounded. Constants the user supplied (the target width, the confidence level, the loss constants) are shown as supplied, to at most 7 significant digits.

...

Not used.

width

The line width, in characters, at which print() wraps the text (not a confidence interval width). Default: nine tenths of getOption("width").

Value

seq_report() returns an object of class c("smsd_report", "character"): a single character string holding the paragraph, with the attributes reference (a character vector with the full reference for the procedure; of length zero when the method label is not known) and method (the method label of x). Use as.character() for the bare string.

print() shows the paragraph, wrapped to width characters, followed by the reference, and returns its input invisibly. format() returns the bare paragraph as a plain character vector of the same length as its input (one string), so a report can be held in a column of a data frame.

Details

Given a check object, the paragraph describes that one check: the rule was met at the current sample size, or it has not yet been met. Whether the current sample size is the first at which the rule was met is something only the user's sampling record can say. Given a path from seq_path, the paragraph describes the stopping stage (the first sample size at which the rule was met or, when it was never met, the last stage checked) and adds where checking began and how often the rule was checked.

For an AIPE result whose confidence level is asymptotic, the paragraph states that satisfying the width criterion does not establish nominal coverage at the observed sample size. The simulation vignette vignette("coverage-and-design", package = "SMSD") gives operating characteristics for difficult designs.

The paragraph is a starting point. It reports what the object holds and cannot know how the data were collected, so read it against the study before using it. Notes carried by the object are appended, each introduced by "Note:". One such note says that the variance estimate was zero, negative, or not finite at that sample size, so that no variance had yet been estimated and the stopping rule was reported as not met (see smsd_check_methods). For an object flagged in that way (its attribute variance_unusable is TRUE) the paragraph gives the estimate without the criterion sample size and without a confidence interval, because neither rests on an estimated variance; the object still holds what the check function returned. For a path, the paragraph also says at how many of the stages before the one it reports the variance estimate was unusable, because the published stopping rules do not set such stages aside.

The procedure and its reference are looked up from the method label of the object. The sources credited are Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018) for the sequential accuracy in parameter estimation procedures for the coefficient of variation, the standardized mean, the standardized mean difference, the regression slope, and the contrast; Chattopadhyay and De (2016) for the Gini index; Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2019) for the correlation coefficients and the squared multiple correlation coefficient; Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2016, 2017) for the minimum risk procedures for the coefficient of variation and the standardized mean difference; Chattopadhyay, Bandyopadhyay, Kelley, and Padalunkal (2025) for the budget constrained procedure; and Mukhopadhyay and de Silva (2009) for the classical procedures. An object whose label is not known to the package is still reported, without a citation and without a reference. The constants of a risk based procedure are reported when the object carries them, under the attributes loss_A (the loss constant), cost_c or cost_1 and cost_2 (the sampling cost), risk_bound, and, where the procedure has them, k (the power of the estimation error in the loss) and t (the power of the sample size in the cost). A width is reported as the target full width of the confidence interval, except for a procedure that bounds the length of its interval and does not aim at a width (the bounded length interval for a median), where it is reported as the largest length allowed.

Sampling under the budget constrained procedure ends in one of three ways, and the paragraph says which: every group reached its criterion sample size, the budget could not pay for another observation from a group still below its criterion, or the data in hand already cost more than the budget. The second is reported as what it is, with the amount of the budget left and the total of the criterion sample sizes that was not reached (left out when the variance of a group could not be estimated), and never as a stopping rule that was met; the third with what the data cost and the budget. The paragraph reads these endings from the attributes rule_met, budget_exhausted, and budget_exceeded that seq_budget sets, and the amounts from budget and remaining_budget; for a budget constrained check without them it says only that sampling ended, which is true of every ending. The note of seq_budget that says the budget is spent, or already exceeded, is not appended when the paragraph has given the amounts, since it would say the same again.

References

Kelley, K., Darku, F. B., & Chattopadhyay, B. (2018). Accuracy in parameter estimation for a general class of effect sizes: A sequential approach. Psychological Methods, 23(2), 226–243. doi:10.1037/met0000127

Kelley, K., Darku, F. B., & Chattopadhyay, B. (2019). Sequential accuracy in parameter estimation for population correlation coefficients. Psychological Methods, 24(4), 492–515. doi:10.1037/met0000203

Chattopadhyay, B., & Kelley, K. (2016). Estimation of the coefficient of variation with minimum risk: A sequential method for minimizing sampling error and study cost. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 51(5), 627–648. doi:10.1080/00273171.2016.1203279

Chattopadhyay, B., & Kelley, K. (2017). Estimating the standardized mean difference with minimum risk: Maximizing accuracy and minimizing cost with sequential estimation. Psychological Methods, 22(1), 94–113. doi:10.1037/met0000089

Chattopadhyay, B., Bandyopadhyay, T., Kelley, K., & Padalunkal, J. J. (2025). A sequential approach for noninferiority or equivalence of a linear contrast under cost constraints. Psychological Methods, 30(2), 425–439. doi:10.1037/met0000570

Chattopadhyay, B., & De, S. K. (2016). Estimation of Gini index within pre-specified error bound. Econometrics, 4(3), 30. doi:10.3390/econometrics4030030

Mukhopadhyay, N., & de Silva, B. M. (2009). Sequential methods and their applications. Chapman & Hall/CRC. ISBN:9780367386535

See also

seq_path; smsd_check_methods for the other methods of a check object.

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

set.seed(113)
# Engagement after a training program against a control group.
trained <- rnorm(100, mean = 4.8, sd = 0.9)
control <- rnorm(100, mean = 4.5, sd = 0.9)

# One check, on the data collected so far.
out <- seq_aipe_smd(trained, control, width = 0.60)
seq_report(out)
#> Sample size was determined with the sequential accuracy in parameter
#> estimation procedure for the standardized mean difference (Kelley,
#> Darku, & Chattopadhyay, 2018), with a target full width of 0.6 for the
#> 95% confidence interval. The stopping rule was met at n = 100 per
#> group. At that sample size the estimate of the standardized mean
#> difference was 0.483, 95% CI [0.198, 0.768]. The confidence level is
#> asymptotic; meeting the width target does not establish nominal
#> coverage at this sample size.
#> 
#> Reference
#> Kelley, K., Darku, F. B., & Chattopadhyay, B. (2018). Accuracy in
#>     parameter estimation for a general class of effect sizes: A
#>     sequential approach. Psychological Methods, 23(2), 226–243.
#>     doi:10.1037/met0000127

# A path: the report describes the first sample size at which the rule
# was met, and says how often the rule was checked.
path <- seq_path(seq_aipe_smd, list(trained, control), width = 0.60,
                 by = 5)
report <- seq_report(path, digits = 2)
report
#> Sample size was determined with the sequential accuracy in parameter
#> estimation procedure for the standardized mean difference (Kelley,
#> Darku, & Chattopadhyay, 2018), with a target full width of 0.6 for the
#> 95% confidence interval. The stopping rule was evaluated from the pilot
#> sample size (n = 7 per group) onward, after every 5 additional
#> observations per group, and was first met at n = 92 per group. At that
#> sample size the estimate of the standardized mean difference was 0.52,
#> 95% CI [0.22, 0.82]. The confidence level is asymptotic; meeting the
#> width target does not establish nominal coverage at this sample size.
#> 
#> Reference
#> Kelley, K., Darku, F. B., & Chattopadhyay, B. (2018). Accuracy in
#>     parameter estimation for a general class of effect sizes: A
#>     sequential approach. Psychological Methods, 23(2), 226–243.
#>     doi:10.1037/met0000127
attr(report, "reference")
#> [1] "Kelley, K., Darku, F. B., & Chattopadhyay, B. (2018). Accuracy in parameter estimation for a general class of effect sizes: A sequential approach. Psychological Methods, 23(2), 226–243. doi:10.1037/met0000127"
